summary: Defines the NAS-Filter-Rule attribute for RADIUS. RFC 2865 only lets a server name a filter that the network access server already has configured. This attribute lets the server send the actual filter rules directly, which helps when the operator does not know what the access server has preinstalled. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A door guard usually has a list of rules written down already. This lets the boss hand the guard new rules on the spot, so the boss does not have to guess what the guard already knows.

subtitle: A RADIUS attribute that carries actual packet filter rules to an access server instead of just naming a preconfigured filter.

tldr.problem: The RADIUS Filter-Id attribute only names a filter that the Network Access Server must already have, which fails when the server operator does not know what was preloaded.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4849 defines attribute 92, NAS-Filter-Rule, whose string holds filter rules in the Diameter IPFilterRule syntax, with rules separated by a NUL octet and split across attributes at 253 octets.
tldr.outcome: A RADIUS server can send explicit filter rules in Access-Accept, CoA-Request or Accounting-Request packets, and Diameter gateways can translate them to and from the Diameter AVP.

today: RFC 4849 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on RFC 2865 for RADIUS and RFC 4005 for the Diameter side.

sections.title: Introduction and Terms
sections.content:
RFC 4849 defines the NAS-Filter-Rule attribute for RADIUS. It has the same functionality as the Diameter NAS-Filter-Rule AVP (400) from RFC 4005 and the same syntax as an IPFilterRule from RFC 3588, Section 4.3.

The motivation is a limit in RFC 2865. Its Filter-Id attribute (11) requires the Network Access Server (NAS) to be pre-populated with the desired filters. When the server operator does not know which filters are preloaded, it is more useful to specify the filter rules explicitly.

The document uses three terms. A NAS is a device that provides an access service for a user to a network. A RADIUS server provides an authentication service to a NAS. A RADIUS proxy acts as an authentication server to the NAS and as a RADIUS client to the RADIUS server.
sections.eli5: Before, the boss could only say "use rule list number 5", which works only if the guard has a list number 5. Now the boss can write the rules out.

sections.title: The Attribute Format
sections.content:
The attribute has three fields: Type is 92, Length is at least 3, and String is one or more octets.

The String holds filter rules in IPFilterRule syntax, with individual rules separated by a NUL octet (0x00). One attribute may hold a partial rule, one rule or several rules. Rules can continue across attribute boundaries, so an implementation cannot assume that a rule begins or ends where an attribute does.

A sender SHOULD concatenate all the rules, separated by NUL octets, and split the result on 253-octet boundaries to get the set of attributes. A receiver concatenates the contents of all NAS-Filter-Rule attributes and then splits on NUL to recover the rules.
sections.eli5: If the list of rules is too long for one envelope, you cut it into pieces and use several envelopes. The reader tapes the pieces back together and reads the rules in order.

sections.title: Where and How It Is Used
sections.content:
Zero or more NAS-Filter-Rule attributes MAY be sent in Access-Accept, CoA-Request or Accounting-Request packets. The attribute table marks them as 0+ in those three packet types and 0 (MUST NOT be present) in Access-Request, Access-Reject and Access-Challenge.

Where several attributes appear, their String fields are concatenated to form one set of rules. RFC 2865 forbids a forwarding server from changing the order of attributes of the same type, so proxies will not reorder them.

The attribute is not meant to be used with other filter attributes. NAS-Filter-Rule and NAS-Traffic-Rule MUST NOT appear in the same packet, and if a NAS-Traffic-Rule is present, a NAS implementing this RFC MUST silently discard the NAS-Filter-Rule attributes. Filter-Id and NAS-Filter-Rule SHOULD NOT appear together, because without defined precedence rules the NAS behavior is undefined.

If a conforming NAS gets an Access-Accept with a NAS-Filter-Rule it cannot apply, it MUST act as though it had received an Access-Reject. For a CoA-Request with an unsupported attribute, the NAS replies with a CoA-NAK, and an Error-Cause attribute of 401 (Unsupported Attribute) is RECOMMENDED. Authorization changes are atomic, so the session continues with its existing configuration.
sections.eli5: The rules slip can ride along with the "you may come in" message. If the guard cannot understand a rule, the guard acts as if the answer was no, rather than letting someone in with the wrong rules.

sections.title: Diameter Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 4005 defines the Diameter NAS-Filter-Rule AVP (400). Diameter/RADIUS gateways need to be configured to translate RADIUS attribute 92 to that AVP and back.

Going from Diameter to RADIUS, the gateway concatenates the individual rules with NUL separators and SHOULD split the data at 253-octet boundaries. Going from RADIUS to Diameter, it joins all attributes, splits on NUL, and encodes each rule as its own Diameter AVP.

A translated Diameter message can exceed the maximum RADIUS packet size of 4096 bytes. In that case the gateway answers the Diameter peer with a Result-Code of DIAMETER_RADIUS_AVP_UNTRANSLATABLE (5018) and a Failed-AVP containing the NAS-Filter-Rule AVP. Repairing this probably needs the filter rules reworked, so the originating peer should treat it as a terminal error.
sections.eli5: Two offices speak slightly different languages. A translator at the border turns one long rule list into pieces, or pieces into a list. If the list is too big for the other side's envelopes, the translator sends it back saying it cannot be done.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The attribute rides in existing RADIUS packets, which are protected as described in RFC 3579 and RFC 3576. RADIUS and Diameter security aims to stop spoofing and modification in transit. It does not stop an authorized server or proxy from changing, inserting or removing attributes with bad intent. If a proxy strips filters, a user could get network access without the right filters, and if it also alters accounting packets, the accounting logs would not show it.

RADIUS has no capability negotiation, so a server cannot discover on its own whether a NAS supports this attribute. A legacy NAS may silently discard it and still let the user in, giving unfiltered access. Therefore NAS-Filter-Rule SHOULD only be sent to a NAS that is known to support it.
sections.eli5: If a middleman tears up the rules slip, the guard lets people in without the rules. And an old guard who does not know about slips may just ignore them, so only hand slips to guards you know can read them.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC creates no new registries. It uses the RADIUS namespace, where one value was allocated in the RADIUS Attribute Types registry: 92 for NAS-Filter-Rule.

It also uses the Diameter namespace, where a Result-Code value for DIAMETER_RADIUS_AVP_UNTRANSLATABLE was allocated. Because this is a permanent failure, the value 5018 is in the 5xxx range.
sections.eli5: The number 92 was reserved for this new kind of slip, and 5018 for the "cannot translate this" answer, so nobody else uses them.
